Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that drives an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix over the GPIO bus, using the row anodes on GPIO 17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM) and the column cathodes on GPIO 5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20 (BCM), scanning each row with an 800 µs delay, lighting an LED by setting the corresponding row HIGH and column LOW, and rendering two wave‑like animations that shift each frame, one moving left‑to‑right and the other right‑to‑left; the program must check every driver call, print descriptive error messages to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle a graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing all GPIO lines and performing cleanup, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75031 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends each reading to a file named depth_log.csv, creating a CSV header row if the file is newly created and writing timestamped distance values; the program must verify successful initialization of the sensor interface, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C read/write transaction, and all file operations, and if an I2C read fails it must log a row with distance ‑1, attempt to re‑open the I2C handle, and continue sampling, while also handling SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates the sensor interface without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to periodically read the distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, verifying the sensor’s presence at startup by reading its model ID register and confirming it matches the documented value, and exiting cleanly with an error message if the read fails or the ID mismatches; after successful initialization the program must poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with roughly a 100 ms timeout, obtain a distance measurement, and every 500 ms print to stdout a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm”, while checking every I2C call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure, issuing a warning to stderr and continuing to the next iteration for any read/write error that occurs during the loop; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, invoking the library’s cleanup call, and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the 16‑bit proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) and logs the values to the console every 500 ms, while checking each driver library or I2C call for errors, detecting a sensor‑absent condition by a NACK on the initial write, handling any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C cleanly closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s API call() for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus 1 device file (/dev/i2c-1) with full error checking, sets the Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor as the I2C slave using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and verifies that the device responds, then enters a loop that every 500 ms (using nanosleep) reads the distance measurement from the sensor and prints a line to stdout in the form “Distance: <value> mm”; if an I2C read fails the program must write a diagnostic message to stderr and simply continue to the next cycle without exiting, while if the sensor is not present at startup it must print an error and exit with status 1; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and terminates the program with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a range profile from a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar over UART (/dev/serial0), decodes each data frame marked by an 8‑byte magic word header followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data representing 64 little‑endian 16‑bit distance bins, checks whether any bin indicates a target within a 1.0‑meter distance threshold, and on detection logs an intrusion entry containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters to a comma‑separated file named intrusion_log.csv, while also activating an alert LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds; the program must handle UART initialization errors using the POSIX driver library, validate all I/O operations, gracefully manage sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17, where the sensor presents an active‑low signal (0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise), and drives a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active‑high) such that the buzzer is activated whenever an obstacle is detected and deactivated when the obstacle is removed; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms via the GPIO bus, log each state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named obstacle_log.txt, rigorously check all driver return values and handle any errors such as chip open failure, line request failure, or read/write errors, and also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and closes the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the distance measurement every 100 ms, logs each distance together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt, and monitors the reading so that when the measured distance falls below 10.0 cm the program asserts a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17); the implementation must handle all I2C read/write errors, detect the absence of the sensor, and manage any errors that occur while creating or writing the log file, and it must also cleanly release all resources—including I2C handles, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking‑assistance system using the STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms in the main loop, check the return code of every driver, I2C, and file operation, and for each measurement append a line “timestamp,distance_mm” to a file named distance_log.csv, creating the file with a header row “timestamp,distance_mm” only when it does not already exist, while also printing a parking guidance message to stdout based on the measured distance—‘STOP’ for less than 300 mm, ‘APPROACH’ for 300‑600 mm, ‘SLOW’ for 600‑1200 mm, and ‘CLEAR’ for greater than 1200 mm; the application must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and de‑initialises the sensor driver on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense CH201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) every 100 ms, logs each timestamped distance and the corresponding LED blink frequency to stdout, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 18 (BCM) through a 330 Ω current‑limiting resistor to 3.3 V so that the LED blinks faster as the measured distance decreases, with each loop iteration performing exactly one half‑cycle of the LED blink (on or off) to keep the blinking smooth across samples; the program must check every driver and I2C call, retry any failed I2C read or write up to three times with 10 ms delays, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent conditions (I2C open failure) and bus‑error paths, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on termination cleanly close the I2C handle, turn off the LED, and shut down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 100 ms sampling interval, triggering each measurement with the required write command, waiting the appropriate delay, then reading the 2‑byte distance value in centimeters, and appending each reading to a comma‑separated file named distance_log.csv formatted as “timestamp,distance_cm”; the program must include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, or read/write timeouts, implement retry logic for transient errors, log any errors to stderr, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two TCRT5000 IR obstacle avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 27 (physical pin 13, BCM), polls each sensor every 10 ms, applies a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and logs every state transition to a file named proximity_log.txt with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type ('DETECTED' for a HIGH‑to‑LOW transition indicating an obstacle and 'CLEARED' for a LOW‑to‑HIGH transition indicating clearance); the program must check the return values of the library’s API call() three times as required, verify all file I/O operations, and on all exit paths—including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM—ensure clean resource release by closing the log file and calling the library’s API call() to release the GPIO resources.

/*
 * VL53L1X Time-of-Flight Distance Monitor for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   VL53L1X SDA -> GPIO2 (I2C bus 1 SDA)
 *   VL53L1X SCL -> GPIO3 (I2C bus 1 SCL)
 *   VL53L1X VDD -> 3.3 V
 *   VL53L1X GND -> GND

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures differential pressure and temperature from the Sensirion SDP810‑125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, configuring the sensor for continuous measurement by sending the documented command bytes, then every second issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 1 ms before reading the 9‑byte data frame that contains the differential pressure (2 bytes plus CRC‑8), temperature (2 bytes plus CRC‑8) and their respective scale factors (2 bytes plus CRC‑8), validating each CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial and initialization value, converting the raw values with the received scale factors, and appending a line to a comma‑separated file named pressure_log.csv that includes an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the pressure in pascals and the temperature in degrees Celsius, creating a header row if the file is new; the program must check all driver and file I/O operations for errors, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP31 (±500 Pa) differential pressure sensor on I²C bus 1 using the documented I²C address, triggers continuous measurement with the documented command, waits at least 1 ms after the trigger, then reads the six‑byte response (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC), converts the values to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius, and appends a line containing a timestamp, pressure_pa and temperature_c as comma‑separated fields to a file named airflow.log, flushing the file after each write; the sampling interval must be 100 ms, and any I²C write or read failure must be retried up to three times with exponential backoff, using the driver library functions for all sensor interactions, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM via a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on every exit path the program must close the I²C handle, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call().

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces over the I2C bus with a Silicon Labs Si7202 I2C Hall‑effect sensor to measure rotational speed, logging the measured speed and temperature to a file named mag_temp_log.csv at one‑second intervals, creating the file with a header row if it does not already exist, and implementing robust error handling that detects and reports failures during I2C initialization, sensor communication, and file I/O; if a sensor read fails the program must write a line containing NaN values for the missing data and then continue operation, and it must also install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates any driver resources, all while meeting the constraints of a precise rotational speed measurement system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high‑accuracy temperature sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second and appending each reading to a file named temperature_log.txt using the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: <value> C\n”, while checking the return value of every I2C call, handling both sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, attempting to re‑initialize the I2C handle up to three consecutive times on failure before exiting, correctly processing negative temperature values, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C) the program closes the I2C handle and terminates the driver cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads airflow data from a Honeywell HAF Series HAFUHH0025PA3 flow sensor over the I2C bus, sampling once every second, extracting a 14‑bit flow value and a 12‑bit temperature value from a single 4‑byte read using the sensor’s API call (no register pointer write required), handling the first two reads after power‑up which may return stale data, and writing each timestamped measurement in SLPM and °C to a file named flow_log.txt; the program must detect I2C communication failures such as sensor disconnection or bus errors, log any read error, attempt to re‑initialize the I2C handle, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handles, close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that bit‑bangs a single‑wire DHT11 temperature/humidity sensor on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) using the provided API call for microsecond timing, the provided API call for GPIO direction control, the provided API call for reading and writing pin levels, and the provided API call for clean shutdown; the program must generate the start signal by pulling the line low for at least 18 ms, then releasing it so the sensor can respond with an 80 µs low pulse followed by an 80 µs high pulse, after which each of the 40 data bits is transmitted beginning with a 50 µs low period and a high period of about 26‑28 µs for a ‘0’ or about 70 µs for a ‘1’, sampling the sensor no more often than every 2 seconds (the DHT11 minimum interval is 1 s), decode the 40 bits into humidity integer (byte 0), humidity decimal (byte 1, always 0), temperature integer (byte 2), temperature decimal (byte 3, always 0) and verify the checksum, write each successful reading to a file named dht11_readings.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, detect and log timeouts on the start signal, response, and each data bit as well as checksum failures and sensor‑absent conditions such as a line stuck high or low, recording each error with a timestamp and a status code, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM release the GPIO resources via the library’s cleanup API, close any open file handles, and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT31-D sensor on the I2C bus using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1), waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the measurement command and logging a new reading every 5 seconds to a file named sht31d_data.log with ISO‑8601 timestamps in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,temperature,humidity”, while checking that the driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C interface opens, that the log file opens, and that each I2C write, I2C read and CRC‑8 validation (using the documented polynomial and initial value) succeed, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times and, if the sensor continues to fail, logging the error with a timestamp and continuing operation, and finally handling SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library; the program must read exactly six bytes per measurement (two bytes temperature plus one CRC, two bytes humidity plus one CRC) and validate each CRC‑8 as specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads two Analog Devices ADPD105 photometric front‑end sensors on the I2C bus, computes the correlated color temperature (CCT) from the sensor data, and logs the average CCT once per second to a file named cct_log.csv, creating the file with a header line “Timestamp,Average_CCT” if it does not already exist; the implementation must use the sensor’s API calls or equivalent block reads for register access, verify the success of every I2C read and write operation, and on any sensor‑absent or bus‑error condition gracefully log an error to stderr and skip that cycle’s entry, while ensuring that all I2C handles, file streams and any driver resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the absolute pressure and temperature from a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over the I2C bus, performing a read cycle every 2 seconds, and appends each measurement together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt; the program must check the result of every driver library or I2C call, and if the sensor is absent, the bus reports an error, or a read fails, it must log the error with a timestamp instead of silently skipping, and it must ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, SIGINT, and SIGTERM—it cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the sensor library’s cleanup API, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the temperature from an STMicroelectronics LM75B sensor on the I2C bus once every second, stores the last 60 samples in a circular buffer in memory, computes the running average, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan is turned on when the average exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off when it falls below 26.0 °C; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C interface, each I2C read, and each GPIO write, logging any failures to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the fan, closing the I2C handle, and terminating the driver library cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from an STTS2004 temperature sensor on the I2C bus, logs the temperature to stdout once per second, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the LED is set high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C; the program must check the result of every I2C read and every GPIO operation, and on repeated I2C failures it must log the errno details and exit cleanly, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all driver library resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, turning the LED off, and then exiting.

/*
 * Si7021 temperature & humidity logger for Raspberry Pi 4 Model B.
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   Si7021 SDA  -> GPIO2 (BCM, I2C bus 1)
 *   Si7021 SCL  -> GPIO3 (BCM, I2C bus 1)
 *   Si7021 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   Si7021 GND  -> GND
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o si7021_logger si7021_logger.c -lsb1
 *
 * The Si7021 has no register addresses; commands are raw byte transfers
 * that the sensor responds to with a 2-byte data word.  We use the
 * "Measure Temperature from Previous RH Measurement" command (0x36,0x0B)
 * and the "Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold" command (0x36,0x14)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 20 ms after each trigger to allow conversion, and appends a line to enviro_log.txt every 5 seconds in the format “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent”; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus with error checking, gracefully handle any I2C communication failures or a missing sensor by skipping the log entry on error, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle and terminate the driver, running in an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the temperature from a Sensirion STS40 I2C temperature sensor on the I2C bus, waiting 10 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and sampling the value every 5 seconds, logging each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named temperature_log.txt; the program must open the I2C device with open(), set the slave address using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read exactly three bytes (two data bytes and one CRC8 byte), verify the CRC8 using the Sensirion‑specified polynomial, and on any error condition—including failures to open the device, ioctl, read, write, CRC mismatch, or open the log file—print a descriptive message to stderr and then continue looping; it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, and run indefinitely in an infinite loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors air‑duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system using the Sensirion SDP810‑500Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting at least 50 ms, then reading the 9‑byte result (2 bytes pressure, 1 byte CRC, 2 bytes temperature, 1 byte CRC, 3 bytes scale factor) once per second, validating every I2C read and write as well as each CRC‑8 using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor, logging each successful sample to a file named hvac_pressure_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C, and on any I2C or CRC error writing an error line with the timestamp and continuing, checking the return of every initialization call (the two required library API calls and fopen) and exiting with an error message if any fails, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API function before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the measurement to complete and sampling once per second, reading the required nine bytes (two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC, and two bytes of scale factor followed by a CRC), validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each successful sample to a file named sdp810_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C; the program must handle I2C open, write, and read errors as well as CRC failures by logging the error and continuing operation, and it must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt closes the I2C handle, terminates any driver resources, closes the log file, and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor on the I2C bus, initializing the driver library and opening the I2C bus with proper error checking, then in a loop triggered every 5 seconds waits 10 ms after each trigger before reading the sensor, appends each sample to a file named environmental_data.txt in append mode flushing after each write, prefixes each line with an ISO 8601 timestamp and also prints the reading to stdout, handling any I2C read/write errors by printing a message to stderr and skipping that sample, and installs a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, after which the program closes the I2C handle, closes the file, and calls the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C, retrieving exactly six bytes per read (two pressure bytes, two temperature bytes, and two CRC bytes) while checking every I2C syscall for errors, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and verifying the CRC on each sensor read; after each trigger a 20 ms delay must be observed, the sensor should be polled once per second, and the result used to drive a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) where the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions and switches to a 5 Hz pattern (100 ms on, 100 ms off) whenever the measured pressure falls below 95 000 Pa, with the GPIO line requested, set to output, and toggled accordingly; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that safely closes the I2C file descriptor and releases the GPIO line before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient and object temperature from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus, logs the timestamped readings to a file named temperature_log.txt every 2 seconds, and controls a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan turns on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and turns off when it falls below 28 °C; the program must validate driver library initialization, opening the I2C bus, and each I2C read/write operation, retrying any failed read up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts and skipping logging for invalid readings, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the Sensirion SHT40 sensor on I2C bus 1, issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 10 ms, then reading exactly six bytes, and streams the live temperature and humidity values to a local HTTP server on port 8080 using the library’s API call to serve an HTML page that displays the current temperature and humidity while clamping humidity to the range 0‑100 %; the implementation must include robust error handling for I2C communication such as sensor absence or bus errors with up to three retries per read, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals appropriately.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs a measurement every 5 seconds, and appends each result to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv with lines formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX”; the program must include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h to compile without warnings, check the success of all initialization and I/O calls, log any read failure to stderr while skipping that entry, and install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl+C is pressed the I2C handle is closed, the driver library is terminated, and the program exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple amplifier and a solid‑state relay, communicating with the MAX6675 over SPI0 (using either CE0 or CE1 as appropriate) and driving the solid‑state relay from GPIO17 (BCM numbering); the program must read the temperature from the thermocouple at a 1 Hz rate, update the SSR duty cycle based on the PID output (scaled 0.0 to 1.0) over a 1‑second period, log each temperature reading to a file named reflow_log.csv, load the target temperature profile from profile.txt where each line contains time_seconds,target_temp_celsius, apply robust error handling for all SPI communication and GPIO control including sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling termination signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled greenhouse heater using a DS18B20 temperature sensor and a 12 V heater driven through a relay and hardware PWM; the DS18B20 data line must be connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7) on the 1‑wire bus accessed via the w1‑gpio kernel module at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, the relay enable line to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), and the PWM duty control to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) using the hardware PWM channel, while the program must accept command‑line arguments specifying the desired temperature setpoint and the PID gains Kp, Ki, and Kd, read the sensor periodically, validate the CRC of each DS18B20 reading and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, compute the PID output, set the appropriate PWM duty cycle and relay state, and log every 5 seconds to a file named greenhouse.log a line containing the timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output and PWM duty cycle; all I/O operations must be checked for errors, and the program must install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that on any exit path cleanly release resources by turning off the relay, setting PWM to zero, closing any opened file descriptors or device handles, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads humidity from an AHT20 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented address, triggering a measurement, waiting 80 ms, then reading the 6‑byte result while verifying that the status byte reports calibrated and not busy, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms pause between attempts, and logging each humidity reading together with a timestamp to the console; the program must poll the sensor every 5 seconds, activate a dehumidifier relay connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the humidity exceeds 60 % and deactivate it when the humidity falls below 55 %, handle the case where the sensor is absent or all retries fail by printing an error message to stderr without terminating, and respond to SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the relative humidity from an HTU21D sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented I2C address, polls the sensor every 60 seconds, and posts the reading as a JSON document to http://api.example.com/humidity via an HTTP POST implemented with standard POSIX sockets; the program must employ syslog for all logging, include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as NACKs, bus errors, CRC mismatches, or sensor absence as well as for any HTTP transmission errors, and must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that cleanly closes all open file descriptors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor on I2C‑1, using the documented I2C address, first verifying that the chip ID matches the documented value, then applying the Bosch compensation formulas to obtain pressure readings; the program must wait approximately 10 ms after each trigger for conversion completion, sample the sensor every 2 seconds, and record any pressure values that exceed 1020 hPa or fall below 980 hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt with timestamps, while handling I2C errors gracefully by attempting up to three retries that re‑open the bus and re‑verify the chip ID, and must include signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s call() function on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that reads temperature from a TMP117, humidity from an AHT20, and motion detection from a PIR motion sensor, logging the values to daily timestamped CSV files with a header line “Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected”; the TMP117 and AHT20 are connected on /dev/i2c-1, the PIR sensor is accessed via the library’s API call on line 17 and is wired to GPIO17 (gpiochip4 line 17, input), the program must sample every 1 second, retry I2C reads up to three times with a 10 ms backoff on failure, create a new log file at midnight each day, print a warning but continue if a sensor is not present at startup, handle I2C errors as described, and ensure all resources are cleanly released on every exit path including SIGINT and SIGTERM, building the code with gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt while using the documented I2C addresses for the TMP117 and AHT20.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a YL‑83 rain sensor connected to GPIO17 (active‑low) via the GPIO bus, polling the sensor every 2 seconds, and when rain is detected commands an L298N motor driver to close a window by driving the motor forward for exactly 5 seconds using ENA on GPIO22, IN1 on GPIO23 and IN2 on GPIO24, then stops the motor; each detection, motor start, motor stop, and any error condition must be logged to stdout with a timestamp, the code must check the return status of every driver call and explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so that on program termination the motor is safely stopped and all GPIO lines are released, while deliberately excluding any DHT22 or humidity sensing functionality.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that modulates a common‑anode RGB LED connected on the GPIO bus with the red cathode on GPIO17, the green cathode on GPIO22, and the blue cathode on GPIO27, sampling the system every 500 ms to read the CPU load from /proc/stat by comparing successive samples and mapping the 0‑100 % load to a color gradient where 0 % is green (0,255,0), 50 % is yellow (255,255,0) and 100 % is red (255,0,0), using hardware PWM via the driver library to set PWM values clamped to 0‑255 for each channel, handling driver library initialization failures by printing an error to stderr and exiting with code 1, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED off (all channels full off for a common‑anode LED) and cleanly invoke the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor on I2C‑1 (SDA = GPIO2/pin 3, SCL = GPIO3/pin 5) using the documented I2C address, waits for each measurement to complete before reading, and every 5 seconds formats the two values into a JSON string and transmits it via UDP to 192.168.1.100 on port 5000; the program must handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions, and UDP send failures gracefully, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly release the I2C handle, close the UDP socket, and shut down the driver library on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that dynamically controls a PWM‑driven cooling fan based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8); the fan PWM must be output on GPIO18 (BCM) using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑255, the program shall read the temperature every 1 second, compute the duty cycle using a piecewise fan curve (0 % below 25 °C, linear ramp from 0 % to 50 % between 25 °C and 40 °C, steeper ramp from 50 % to 200 % between 40 °C and 60 °C, and 100 % above 60 °C), store each timestamp, temperature, and PWM duty cycle in a 20‑entry circular buffer, perform robust error checking for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call); on any SPI transfer error or MAX31855 fault, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle, initialize the driver library and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz mode 0, and on receipt of SIGINT stop the PWM, close the SPI interface, print the full contents of the circular buffer, terminate the driver library and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD‑to‑digital converter over SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 (GPIO8) at 1 MHz, operates the device in 3‑wire RTD mode with the bias voltage enabled, checks the fault status register on each read, computes the temperature using the Callendar‑Van Dusen equation, and logs the results every 5 seconds to a file named rtd_log.csv containing a timestamp and the temperature; the program must include robust error handling that logs SPI communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and any read errors without crashing, and it must perform a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature, humidity and pressure from a BME280 sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL, device file /dev/i2c-1) using the documented I2C address, verifies that the BME280 chip ID matches the documented value during initialization, and then logs a line to a file named bme280_log.csv every five seconds containing a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, the temperature in degrees Celsius, the relative humidity in percent, and the pressure in hectopascals; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all file descriptors and file pointers are cleanly released on any exit path, including when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, employing the library's API call for I2C communication and the library's API call for a hardware timer that triggers every 50 ms; each reading must be stored in a circular buffer sized to hold timestamped pressure values for the last 60 seconds, from which a rolling average is computed, and if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from that average the program shall assert an active‑HIGH alert on GPIO24, logging the alert to stderr, while also logging any I2C failures or sensor absence with robust error handling; the sampling loop must use the library's API call for the 50 ms timer, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release resources by closing the I2C interface, resetting GPIO24, and terminating the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the temperature from an LM75 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs the read once per second, stores each reading in an in‑memory circular buffer of capacity 60 samples protected by a mutex, updates a running average from the buffer, and drives an alert LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) from a background thread so that the LED is turned on whenever the temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the implementation must check the result of every I2C read/write and every GPIO initialization call, log any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions to stderr, attempt to re‑initialize the hardware on such errors, and ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, error paths, and receipt of SIGINT—the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and destroying the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater with a PID loop using a PT100 RTD read through a MAX31865 on SPI0 CE0 configured to mode 1 at 500 kHz, employing a 430‑ohm reference resistor and assuming the PT100 nominal resistance of 100 Ω, where the heater is driven by a MOSFET controlled with hardware PWM on GPIO18 at a 1 kHz frequency using a driver range of 1000 for 0‑100 % duty; the PID loop must execute every 100 ms, loading the target temperature and PID gains from a JSON configuration file at startup with defaults of 25 °C, Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01 if any values are missing, and must implement a failsafe that immediately sets the PWM duty to zero and exits with an error if the temperature exceeds 80 °C, an SPI read fails, or any MAX31865 fault is detected, while also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by turning off the heater, closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver, and exiting cleanly, and logging any errors to stderr and returning a non‑zero exit code on critical failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, sampling once per second, and writes any temperature reading above 30.0 °C or pressure reading below 950 hPa to a file named breach_log.txt with a timestamp for each breach; the program must perform all BMP180 calibration calculations using integer arithmetic only, avoid any floating‑point pow operations, check the result of every system call and retry transient failures up to three times, explicitly handle cases where the sensor is absent or the I2C bus reports an error, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reading and validating the 11‑word calibration table from the documented register before any sampling, and then, via a hardware timer callback that fires every 500 ms, obtains temperature and pressure using the BMP180 formulas with OSS = 0 (ensuring the temperature routine is not called from inside the pressure routine), stores each timestamped reading in a 60‑entry circular buffer, prints each new reading to stdout, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (active‑high) whenever the temperature exceeds 30 °C; the timer callback must remain simple and avoid blocking calls, every library API call’s return code must be checked and the sample skipped on error, and the program must handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces over I2C bus 1 with a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope, performs a 100‑sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X, Y and Z zero‑rate offsets, then continuously reads angular velocity, applies the offsets, and logs the calibrated X, Y, Z values together with ISO‑8601 timestamps to a file named gyro_log.txt at a 20 Hz rate (50 ms period), appending an alert line to the same log whenever any axis exceeds 50 dps and also printing a warning to stderr for the same condition; the program must verify the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect sensor absence by reading the WHO_AM_I register and confirming the documented value, handle any I2C bus errors, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (/dev/i2c-1 character device)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 every 100 ms (10 Hz), verifies that the device ID register returns the documented value before any sampling, and logs each sample to a file named accel_log.txt in the format “timestamp,x,y,z” with the three axis values expressed in g units to three decimal places; the program must configure the ADXL345 for full‑resolution mode with a ±2 g range, check the result of every I2C call and avoid writing any garbage to the log on read failures, turn on an active‑high LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) whenever the absolute acceleration on any axis exceeds 2.0 g and turn it off otherwise, and cleanly release the I2C handle, GPIO, and close the log file when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC accelerometer and magnetometer connected on I2C bus 1, samples the sensors every 100 ms, computes a tilt‑compensated heading, and logs each sample with a timestamp, the heading, the three‑axis acceleration in g, and the three‑axis magnetic field in gauss to a file named compass_log.txt, adding a CSV header when the file is created; the program must check the result of every I2C operation and handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU Ultrasonic MEMS Microphone sensors connected on I2C bus 1 at a 10 ms sampling interval, reads 16‑bit signed audio samples from each sensor, timestamps each pair of samples using CLOCK_REALTIME, computes the time‑difference‑of‑arrival (TDOA) between the two channels, and appends a line to a CSV‑formatted file named audio_log.dat with the columns sec,nsec,sensor1,sensor2,tdoa; the implementation must verify that all driver library initialization and I2C communication calls succeed, and if a sensor is absent or the bus fails it must gracefully skip that sample and retry, while a SIGINT signal handler must guarantee clean release of I2C handles, closure of the log file, and termination of the driver library on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU over SPI0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) using a 1 MHz SPI clock in mode 3 (CPOL = 1, CPHA = 1) with 16‑bit words, respecting a stall time of at least 40 µs between the read request and the data transfer, sampling every 100 ms and attaching millisecond‑precision timestamps; each read consists of a 16‑bit command word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7‑bit register address and the data are returned on the subsequent 16‑bit transfer, and the raw values must be converted using a gyroscope sensitivity of 0.005 deg/sec/LSB and an accelerometer sensitivity of 0.00025 g/LSB before being logged to a file named imu_data.csv with a header row “timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z”, while checking the API call return values and the fopen return value, logging any API call that returns less than 0 to stderr and skipping that sample; the program must install a cleanup() helper with atexit() to close the SPI handle, the CSV file and terminate the driver on all exit paths, handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, and use a non‑blocking delay that checks a running flag every few milliseconds so signals are processed promptly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI bus 0 using chip‑select CS0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in SPI mode 3 with a maximum clock of 1 MHz, reads the gyroscope and accelerometer registers using the single‑register read protocol (send the 8‑bit register address with bit 7 set in the first 16‑bit SPI cycle and capture the 16‑bit data response in the second cycle), applies the gyro scale of 0.02 dps/LSB and accel scale of 0.00025 g/LSB, and logs the six values (gyroscope X, Y, Z and accelerometer X, Y, Z) to the console every 100 ms; the program must include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ioctl transfers, and data reads, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release resources by closing the SPI device file and the driver library chip before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 every 10 ms in full‑resolution mode with a ±2 g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), verifies that the device ID register returns the documented value and checks the result of every I2C read or write, and when the computed total acceleration magnitude exceeds a 2.5 g threshold it turns on a red LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 500 ms, records the event to a file named impact_log.txt with a timestamp and the magnitude together with the X, Y and Z components, and ensures that on normal exit or on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle, the LED GPIO, the log file and any driver state—are cleanly released, while also handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions according to the verification steps.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens I2C bus 1 to communicate with a TDK InvenSense ICM‑20602 IMU, performs burst reads of the six accelerometer bytes and six gyroscope bytes at a 10 Hz rate (every 100 ms), checks the return value of every I2C operation and prints any failures to stderr, timestamps each sample and appends the x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a file named imu_log.csv, and handles Ctrl +C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating the driver library, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer on I2C bus 1, verifies the sensor’s identity by reading its identification register and confirming the documented value before proceeding, polls the sensor every 100 ms, and whenever the magnitude on any axis exceeds the 2.0 g threshold (with the default ±2 g range where 1 g equals 1024 counts) it turns on an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) for 500 ms while logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named impact_log.txt; the program must handle I2C read/write errors gracefully and, on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, cleanly release the I2C bus, GPIO lines and close the log file.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads magnetic field data from a Texas Instruments TMAG5273 I2C 3D Hall‑Effect sensor over the I2C bus at the default sensor address, samples the data once per second, and logs each reading together with a timestamp to a file named magnetic_field_log.csv, creating the file with a header row on startup if it does not already exist; the program must check the result of every system call such as open, ioctl, read, write, fopen and similar, handling any errors gracefully, and if an I2C read fails it should write an error message to stderr and continue the sampling loop, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly closes both the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the SparkFun ADXL345 I2C accelerometer on I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1, wiring the ADXL345 INT1 pin to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering), to detect free‑fall events via a GPIO interrupt, verify the device ID at startup (ensuring the documented value is read), place the sensor in standby mode before any register writes, and on each interrupt capture timestamped acceleration samples (X, Y, Z) only while free‑fall is active, writing them to a file named freefall_log.csv that is created with a header row and uses the format YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm,X,Y,Z with the file flushed after each write; the implementation must check every I2C system call and GPIO operation for errors, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, run a poll‑based loop on the driver’s event file descriptor (no threads), and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly disable the sensor’s interrupts, close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO line, close the sensor device, and close the CSV log file.
