prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU over I2C bus 1 using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM) at a 104 Hz output data rate, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named motion_log.txt, and implements a basic fall‑detection state machine that transitions from IDLE to FREEFALL when the acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g and then to IMPACT when it exceeds 2.5 g within a 1.0 s detection window, while handling I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions verified by a WHO_AM_I check, and other bus errors gracefully, and ensures clean resource release on SIGINT or SIGTERM; the sensor must be configured for a ±2 g accelerometer range and a ±250 dps gyroscope range.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates with an Analog Devices ADIS16266 digital gyroscope over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in SPI mode 3 (CPOL = 1, CPHA = 1) at a 1 MHz clock, performing 16‑bit register accesses with a 2‑byte transfer per register and no dummy byte, sending a read command by OR‑ing the register address with bit 7 and receiving the response in the following transaction, verifying the WHO_AM_I register on startup, and then sampling the angular rate at a 10 ms interval, converting the raw value with the scale factor of 0.0305 deg/sec/LSB, and appending timestamped readings to a single CSV file named gyro_log.csv that is opened once at program start with an appropriate header and never reopened; the code must check the return value of every SPI driver call, print informative error messages on any failure, and handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the SPI handle, terminating the driver, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads angular velocity data from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope on I2C bus 1, sampling every 10 ms, converts the raw values using the 8.75 mdps/LSB sensitivity (divide by 114.285), and appends timestamped records to a file named gyro_log.csv with a header row “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where timestamps are recorded with nanosecond precision; the program must verify that the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register returns the documented value before proceeding, retry any I2C write during initialization up to three times, check the result of every I2C call and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions appropriately, and on receipt of SIGINT perform graceful termination by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output (DO) of a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) on the GPIO bus every 500 ms, enables the internal pull‑up resistor on that line because the sensor’s open‑collector output is active‑LOW (LOW indicates flame, HIGH indicates no flame), and writes each reading to an append‑mode file named flame_events.log with an immediately flushed line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS – Flame detected: YES” when the pin reads LOW or “… NO” when it reads HIGH; when a flame is detected the program must also print the message “FLAME DETECTED!” to the console, and it must check that the driver initialization succeeded, verify that the log file handle is valid, and treat any sensor read error (e.g., the API returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line instead of a false positive; a SIGINT handler should be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C sets a flag that cleanly exits the polling loop, and on any exit path the program must close the log file if open and call the library’s cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an Omron D7S‑0001 vibration sensor over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, samples the X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms, and appends each sample to a file named vibration_log.csv with a header line “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where the timestamp is an ISO‑8601 UTC string; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, and read call, detect the documented sensor‑absent condition (for example when an I2C read returns the documented error value or fails), handle any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and on a read failure print a diagnostic message to stderr and simply skip that sample, while a SIGINT handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before the program exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors two TI DRV5032 digital Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Hall sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Hall sensor 2 to GPIO27 (BCM), configuring both inputs with internal pull‑ups enabled via bias flags, logging the millisecond‑precision timestamped state of each sensor to a file named conveyor_log.txt every 50 ms, and when both sensors read logic 1 the program must simulate halting the conveyor by printing a halt message; the implementation must include robust error handling for all GPIO access operations such as opening the chip, requesting lines, and reading values as well as for file I/O, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that continuously polls a GY‑45 MMA8452Q 3‑axis accelerometer on I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 at roughly 100 Hz (a 10 ms loop interval), first verifying the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register and exiting with an error message if the returned value does not match the documented value, then initializing the device by reading the control register, placing the sensor in standby, configuring the data rate to 100 Hz, and re‑enabling active mode; the program must read the six data registers in a single block read, combine the MSB and LSB of each axis, right‑shift by four to obtain signed 12‑bit raw X, Y, and Z values, compute the absolute tilt and, when a tilt exceeding 45 degrees is detected, append a line to a file named fall_log.txt (opened once in append mode at startup and flushed after each entry) containing a timestamp and the three raw values; all I2C system calls (open, ioctl, read, write) must be checked for failure with strerror(errno) printed and the appropriate action taken (exit or skip the iteration), and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must be installed to close both the I2C file descriptor and the log file before terminating.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that configures SPI channel 0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in Mode 0 with a 1 MHz clock to communicate with an Analog Devices ADXL354B accelerometer, performs the documented reset sequence by writing the required value to the reset register, waiting 1 ms, clearing the RUN bit in the power‑control register, waiting until the STABLE bit in the status register is set, and then setting the RUN bit, verifies sensor presence by reading the PARTID and confirming the documented value, then repeatedly reads the 20‑bit signed X, Y, and Z acceleration data (three consecutive bytes per axis) using SPI reads with bit 7 = 1 for read and bit 6 = 1 for multi‑byte, logs each set of readings together with a timestamp to a file named vibration_log.txt at 100 ms intervals, implements retry logic for any SPI communication errors, and includes a graceful shutdown handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM that cleanly closes the SPI device, closes the log file, and terminates any driver resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM), operating at a 1 MHz baud rate in SPI Mode 3 (active‑high clock, sampled on the trailing edge) with the required 16‑bit read protocol of sending the address byte with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte and receiving the data on the next 16‑bit transfer, scaling the gyroscope output by 0.05 deg/sec per LSB and the accelerometer output by 0.0025 g per LSB, sampling at approximately 100 Hz by inserting a 10 ms delay between reads, and logging each timestamped measurement to a file named imu_log.csv that begins with the header “Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel” and records high‑precision UNIX epoch timestamps in seconds.nanoseconds; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the SPI device, opening of the CSV file, and the return codes of each library API call, printing any API error to stderr and skipping that iteration, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) via a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the library’s cleanup API before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected on the GPIO bus, reading the sensor output from GPIO17 on gpiochip4 (BCM numbering) once every second, and when the sensor reports a LOW level indicating an obstacle within the configured ~30 cm detection range, logs to the console with timestamps the messages “Self‑parking sequence started” and, after the simulated routine completes, “Self‑parking sequence completed”; the implementation must use modern driver library APIs for opening the chip, requesting the line, reading its value and releasing resources, must check the return status of every library call and, if any call or the line is unavailable, exit gracefully with an appropriate error message, and must also install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C triggers a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO line and closes the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls two Keyes KY‑032 IR obstacle‑avoidance sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and sensor 2 to GPIO27 (physical pin 13), using a single bulk‑read API call that reads both lines together at a 100 ms interval, interprets the active‑low output (0 = obstacle detected, 1 = path clear), logs the detection status together with a timestamp to the console on each poll, checks the return value of every driver call and handles the case where the API call or the GPIO lines are unavailable, runs in an infinite loop until interrupted, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C)—performs clean release of all resources, while compiling cleanly with ‑Wall ‑Wextra against driver version 2.0 or newer.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 over the SPI bus using SPI0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) at a 1 MHz clock, operating in SPI Mode 3 with MSB‑first transmission on the /dev/spidev0.0 device, employing a two‑transfer read protocol where the address byte is sent with the MSB set followed by a 2‑byte read, then applying the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec per LSB to obtain X, Y, and Z angular rates, logging those rates to the console every 100 ms, checking all SPI and GPIO initialization calls and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including when a SIGINT is received.
pinned_library: libgpiod for the SPI CS line, with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU, reading the accelerometer and gyroscope X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms and printing a single line containing the six values to stdout for each sample; the program must check the return value of every I2C operation, handle driver library initialization failure, I2C device open failure, WHO_AM_I register mismatch, any register write failures, and short or failed burst reads by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, avoid using hard‑coded sleeps that ignore errors, and install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls the appropriate library cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens I2C bus 1 on the SDA pin (GPIO2, BCM) and SCL pin (GPIO3, BCM) to communicate with an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board, first confirming the device is present by reading its identification register and comparing the result to the documented value, then initializing the sensor and entering a loop that every 100 ms reads a 12‑byte combined block containing six bytes of 14‑bit left‑aligned accelerometer data followed by six bytes of 16‑bit magnetometer data, extracts the raw X, Y, Z values for both the accelerometer and magnetometer and prints them to the console, while checking each I2C call for errors, retrying on transient read failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle and any driver state—are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C, evaluates the tilt angle and, whenever the tilt exceeds a threshold of 30.0 degrees, writes a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log, performing this sampling and logging cycle every 100 ms; the implementation must include robust error handling that explicitly detects and manages I2C communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and bus‑error paths, and must guarantee clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of a Ctrl+C interrupt signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the digital OUT line of a KY‑038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) over successive 5‑second windows, sampling the pin every 1 ms; after each 5‑second window the program must print to stdout a timestamped line either “ALERT” if the count of high readings exceeds a user‑defined threshold or a status line otherwise, then pause for 1 second before starting the next window, accepting a single command‑line argument that is an integer threshold of minimum high‑readings per window and rejecting any non‑numeric or non‑positive values with a clear error printed to stderr; every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for failure and any error reported to stderr; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by terminating the driver usage and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that controls two 12 V electromagnetic door locks via TIP120‑driven 5 V active‑HIGH relay modules on the GPIO bus, using GPIO17 (BCM) for Door A and GPIO27 (BCM) for Door B, both initialized as outputs with a default LOW state that keeps the locks energized/closed and a HIGH level that de‑energizes the relay to unlock the door for exactly 5 seconds; at program start and after each successful entry the application must generate a random six‑digit security code in the range 100000‑999999, print it to stdout, then read user input from stdin, handling non‑numeric input by clearing the buffer and re‑prompting, compare the entered code to the generated one, and on a match log a CSV line “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN” to a file named access_log.txt, while printing “Access denied” and continuing on a mismatch; every driver call that opens the chip, gets a line, or requests a line as well as the file open must be checked, with meaningful error messages sent to stderr and a non‑zero exit on any initialization failure; the program must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on termination it must set both GPIO outputs to LOW (locking the doors), release all driver resources and close any open file handles; the source must compile with gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3) with the ADDR pin tied to GND, waits up to the maximum 180 ms conversion time, and logs a reading every 5 seconds to a file named light_log.txt using the format “Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>”, while handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent (for example failing to open the bus or read bytes), and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 to implement a theremin which, upon receiving an authenticated TCP command on port 12345, plays a PWM tone on hardware PWM pin GPIO18 (BCM) for exactly 5 seconds, sampling the touch values every 20 ms during playback, logging each played frequency to a file named frequency_log.txt, handling errors for the driver initialization, I2C open and read operations, socket creation, bind, listen and accept calls, and performing a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the PWM output, closing the I2C interface and sockets, and terminating the driver library; the TCP message must begin with the string “MOTION_DETECTED:” and contain the shared secret “MySecretKey”, and the MPR121 must be initialized with a proper soft‑reset and electrode configuration before use.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads magnetic field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer over I2C bus 1 using the physical SDA1 and SCL1 pins, samples the sensor every 100 ms by performing a single block read of six bytes beginning at the magnetometer’s first data register, extracts the Z‑axis field magnitude, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) with hardware PWM so that the LED brightness is proportional to that Z‑axis magnitude; the program must handle I2C errors such as a missing sensor or bus faults by logging the error and skipping the current sample without crashing, and it must cleanly release all resources—including stopping PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor and any log files—when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.
pinned_library: libgpiod for GPIO/PWM, with standard Linux I2C (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO‑connected HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor (TRIG on GPIO4 BCM, ECHO on GPIO18 BCM) to measure distance in an interrupt‑driven fashion and log each valid reading to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format “timestamp_ns,distance_cm”, running indefinitely; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse on the TRIG line, wait 200 ms between trigger cycles, capture the echo pulse width with rising‑edge and falling‑edge interrupt callbacks protected by a mutex, discard any measurement whose pulse width exceeds 23 200 µs (approximately 4 m, the sensor’s maximum range), treat a missing echo within 100 ms after a trigger as a timeout error, handle driver library initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths and sensor timeouts, record timestamps with nanosecond precision using a 32‑bit tick counter that wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination cancels the callbacks, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and destroys the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, detects a free‑fall when the measured acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g, then detects an impact when the magnitude rises above 1.5 g (allowing the free‑fall and impact thresholds to be overridden by optional command‑line arguments), and upon detecting the impact activates a buzzer connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly one second; the implementation must initialize the I2C interface and the sensor driver with full error checking, retry any I2C communication failure up to three times, handle the absence of the sensor or bus errors gracefully, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program performs a clean shutdown releasing all resources and leaving the GPIO and I2C bus in a safe state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to drive two 28BYJ‑48 stepper motors with ULN2003 driver boards, configuring Motor 1 (X‑axis) IN1 on GPIO4 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO17 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO27 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO22 (BCM), and Motor 2 (Y‑axis) IN1 on GPIO5 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO6 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO13 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO19 (BCM) as outputs, employing a 4‑step wave drive sequence (single‑coil excitation) with a 1000 µs step delay, calculating the required steps from the 28BYJ‑48’s 1/64 gear ratio and 2048 steps per revolution to trace a 50 mm square, checking that the driver initialization succeeds and verifying each API call, handling any motor movement failures gracefully, and installing a SIGINT handler that safely stops both motors, sets all GPIO pins low and releases resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that generates randomized haptic feedback patterns on two Precision Microdrives 310-101 eccentric rotating mass (ERM) vibration motors connected via GPIO (PWM), with Motor 1 driven on GPIO 17 (BCM) and Motor 2 on GPIO 27 (BCM); each pattern must consist of a sequence of 5 to 15 steps, each step specifying a PWM duty cycle from 0 to 255 for each motor and a step duration between 50 ms and 200 ms, using the appropriate API calls for PWM control and timing, seeding the random number generator with time(NULL), checking the API call return values, verifying that the GPIO mode is set correctly, handling any memory allocation failures, and running indefinitely to generate and play new random patterns until a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received, at which point a volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown flag should trigger a graceful shutdown that stops both motors and releases all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a weight‑triggered solenoid lock using a load cell amplified by an HX711 on the GPIO bus, with the HX711 data line connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the clock line to GPIO17 (BCM), and the solenoid lock driven by GPIO27 (BCM) as an active‑high lock signal; the program must read the HX711 sensor every 500 ms, enforce a read timeout of 0.5 seconds and gracefully skip any iteration where the timeout occurs, initialize the GPIO driver with error checking, load calibration data (scale_factor and offset) from a space‑separated calibration.txt file or fall back to defaults of scale = 1.0 and offset = 0.0 if the file is missing or invalid, perform a one‑time startup calibration by averaging 100 readings at zero load to determine the offset, compute weight using the loaded or default scale and offset, engage the solenoid (set GPIO27 high) when the computed weight exceeds a calibrated threshold of 10.0 kg, log each reading with a timestamp to weight_log.txt and write any updated calibration values back to calibration.txt, and handle SIGINT to cleanly shut down by releasing all GPIO resources and closing open files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, debouncing by taking five readings spaced 50 ms apart and declaring rain when at least three of those readings are LOW (the sensor outputs LOW when rain is present and HIGH when dry); when rain is detected the program must drive a DC motor through an L298N motor driver using IN1 on GPIO17 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO18 (BCM) and the PWM enable line on GPIO27 (BCM), setting IN1 high, IN2 low and applying a 1000 Hz PWM signal with a duty cycle value of 150 (out of 0‑255) for exactly five seconds to close the window, then stopping the motor by clearing IN1, IN2 and PWM, logging each rain event and each motor action with timestamps to /var/log/window_control.log via syslog, checking the sensor only once every 60 seconds and waiting an additional 60 seconds after a closing operation before the next check, handling any GPIO initialization failures with clear error messages and distinct exit codes, providing robust error handling for all sensor reads and motor control actions, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the motor is stopped, all GPIO resources are released, and the log file is properly closed for a graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a kitchen ingredient stock level using a TAL220B load cell amplified by an HX711 connected on the GPIO bus with bit‑banged communication, reading the data line (DT) on GPIO23 (BCM) and the clock line (SCK) on GPIO24 (BCM), checking the weight once every second, and when the measured weight falls below 100 g it must activate a solenoid lock attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly five seconds; each weight check, lock activation, and any error condition—including HX711 read timeouts, a data line stuck high, GPIO operation failures, or file I/O problems—must be logged with a timestamp to a file named stock_events.txt, and the program must implement robust error handling for all reads, writes, and file operations and perform proper resource cleanup when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier using a bit‑banged GPIO bus with the data line on GPIO4 (BCM) and the clock line on GPIO17 (BCM), applying clock high/low delays of at least 1 µs, and obtains raw 24‑bit signed values; at startup the program must prompt the user to place a known weight, compute and save a calibration factor to a file named calibration.txt, then continuously sample the sensor, treating a data line that remains high for more than 100 ms as a communication timeout, and when the calibrated weight exceeds a threshold of 5.0 kg the program must engage a solenoid door lock connected to GPIO27 (BCM) by setting the pin high for exactly 5 seconds before releasing it, log the timestamp and weight to a file called security.log each time the threshold is exceeded, and robustly handle driver initialization failures, file open or write errors, calibration read errors, and HX711 timeouts; a SIGINT handler must be provided to gracefully unlock the solenoid, terminate the driver, close any open files and release all resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keywish KY‑022 IR obstacle avoidance sensor connected to GPIO16 (BCM) on the GPIO bus and toggles a Songle SRD‑05VDC‑SL relay module attached to GPIO20 (BCM) accordingly, logging each state change with the new relay state (ON or OFF) and an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named relay_events.log; the sensor is active‑low so a LOW reading indicates an obstacle and must cause the relay, which is active‑high, to switch from its current state to the opposite state, and the implementation must use only the provided driver library APIs for all GPIO operations, must detect and report initialization failures such as chip not found or line request failed, must detect and report sensor read errors and log file write errors with descriptive messages, must clean up all GPIO resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM before exiting, and must ensure that every toggle event is recorded in the log file as specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, and when the sensor’s active‑high 3.3 V output indicates motion, activates a 5 V buzzer on GPIO18 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds using usleep for timing, then returns the buzzer to the off state; each motion detection must be logged by appending a line with the timestamp in the format YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS to a file named motion_log.txt, and every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for errors so that a missing sensor or bus error causes a clear error message and clean program exit; the program must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn off the buzzer, close the log file, and release all GPIO resources before terminating, and it should run indefinitely until the user presses Ctrl‑C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a timed watering system by activating a Parker Hannifin Series 9 General Purpose Miniature Solenoid Valve (12 V, 1.6 W) through an external N‑channel MOSFET or relay module connected to GPIO18 (BCM) on the GPIO bus; the program must read the watering duration, constrained to 1–3600 seconds, from a configuration file named watering.conf that contains a single line of the form duration=<seconds>, reject empty files, malformed lines, or out‑of‑range values, initialize the GPIO line as an output with active‑low = 0 and a default low value (valve off), activate the valve by setting the line high, wait the configured duration using a signal‑safe interruptible sleep, then set the line low, print status messages to stdout showing the configured duration and each valve on/off transition, perform error handling by checking every driver call for errors and printing descriptive messages to stderr, install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, have the main loop poll this flag and turn the valve off before exiting, and ensure that on every exit path—whether normal completion, signal receipt, or error—the GPIO line is released and the chip closed so the valve is always left off.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls a line‑following robot using a Keywish 3‑Way Infrared Tracking Sensor and two DC motors driven through an L298N motor driver, communicating over the GPIO / PWM bus; the left sensor must be read from GPIO4 (BCM), the middle sensor from GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor from GPIO27 (BCM), and the motor PWM signals must be output on GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24 and GPIO25 (BCM), with all three sensor inputs sampled every 10 ms and the PWM signals generated at a 1 kHz frequency, while the sensors provide active‑low digital signals and the control law requires that when the middle sensor is low the robot drives straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255, when only the left sensor is low the robot turns right by halving the left motor speed, when only the right sensor is low it turns left by halving the right motor speed, and when no sensor is low both motors are stopped; each control cycle must be logged to a file named trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states (0/1), and the left and right motor speeds, and the implementation must include robust error handling for initializing the driver library, opening the log file, and all GPIO operations, and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt stops both motors, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and ensures that all driver library API calls are properly released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads illuminance from a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1, observes a 180 ms measurement delay, and drives a relay connected to GPIO23 (BCM) to turn on a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150, logging each lux value and every relay state change with millisecond‑precision timestamps to a file named grow_log.txt; the program must handle I2C errors gracefully by logging any sensor detection or read failures and continuing operation without crashing, run indefinitely until a SIGINT is received, and on that signal cleanly release all resources by closing the I2C handle, turning off the relay, and terminating the driver library, using only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a door lock using the library's API call to drive a servo motor on the GPIO/PWM bus, with the servo connected to GPIO18 (BCM) and two push‑buttons connected to GPIO21 (BCM) for lock and GPIO22 (BCM) for unlock, both using pull‑up resistors and active‑low logic (reading 0 when pressed); the program must debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay, set the servo pulse width to 1000 µs (≈0°) when the lock button is pressed and to 2000 µs (≈180°) when the unlock button is pressed while respecting the API’s safe pulse‑width range of 500‑2500 µs, print status messages for each action, handle any initialization failures gracefully by printing an error message, and install a SIGINT signal handler that cleanly releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that generates a haptic feedback system by pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310‑101 vibration motors sequentially and repeatedly over the GPIO bus, driving motor 1 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for 200 ms, then motor 2 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for 300 ms, and looping this pattern indefinitely; the design must include robust error handling that checks every driver library call for line request failures and value write failures, as well as proper registration of signal handlers, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully release the GPIO lines and stop the motors by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths, while observing the constraint that the motors require 3 V at 60 mA typical and therefore must be driven through an external driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode rather than being connected directly to the GPIO pins.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a sound‑triggered alarm as a single executable with two selectable modes chosen by a command‑line argument; in the sound_sensor mode the program polls the LM393 sound sensor on its digital output pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM) every 10 ms, treats a logic 0 on this active‑low pin as a sound event, and publishes an alert on a ZeroMQ socket bound to tcp://*:5555 using the topic SOUND_ALERTS, while in the alarm_node mode the program subscribes to tcp://localhost:5555 for the same topic and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second; the implementation must use the GPIO bus directly without any driver library, provide robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses an IR receiver such as the TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) to decode NEC infrared remote signals and report the decoded commands both to syslog and to an MQTT broker at localhost on port 1883 using the topic ir/decoded, publishing the command as a JSON object; the program must register an alert callback on the falling edge of the GPIO to capture pulse timings, interpret the NEC frame consisting of a 9 ms mark followed by a 4.5 ms space header, 560 µs marks for each bit, a 1690 µs space for logic‑1 and a 560 µs space for logic‑0, decode the full 32‑bit frame, validate the command against its inverted copy while allowing extended NEC frames that omit inverted‑address validation, check driver initialization and GPIO setup failures, guard against pulse‑buffer overflow, verify the NEC checksum, initialize the MQTT client once at startup and invoke the network loop in the main loop, and ensure clean release of all resources—including the driver, MQTT client, and syslog—when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light from four BH1750FVI sensors attached to I2C‑1, waiting 180 ms after each start‑conversion command, and repeats this acquisition loop once per second; for each sensor the program must issue an ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before any transaction, may use a single /dev/i2c-1 descriptor or one per sensor, and must not rely on any external driver library, handling any open, address‑set, write, read or partial‑read failure by inserting a NaN value for that sensor while continuing with the others; after gathering the lux values it must broadcast a UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005 containing a semicolon‑separated list of sensor_id,lux pairs such as 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a termination flag so the loop can exit cleanly, ensuring that all file descriptors for I2C and the UDP socket are closed on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, issues a zero‑length I2C write to generate a start condition and then reads two bytes from the Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor, masks the 14‑bit flow value from the first two bytes according to the sensor documentation, converts it to SLPM, and logs a timestamped flow‑rate entry to a file named airflow_log.txt once per second; the program must check the result of every system call, retry any transient I2C read failure up to three times with a 100 ms delay between attempts, and handle the distinct error paths for a missing sensor (ENXIO) and a bus error (EIO), and it must install a SIGINT handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes and closes the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads spectral and lux data from an Adafruit AS7341 10‑Channel Light/Color Sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) for plant health monitoring, verifying that the sensor’s identification register matches the documented value, powering the device on by setting the PON bit in the ENABLE register, configuring the SMUX through the CFG6 register, and enabling spectral measurement with the SP_EN bit, then acquiring all ten spectral channels (F1‑F8, Clear and NIR) every five seconds, computing a simplified lux approximation from those readings, and appending a timestamped, comma‑separated line to spectral_log.csv at the same interval while checking every I2C read/write return value and handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, and finally ensuring that all resources—including the I2C file descriptor and the log file—are cleanly closed on normal termination or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri‑axial acceleration data from an Omron D7S seismic sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and logs the timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to a CSV file named seismic_data.csv by default, with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g, while also writing any error messages with timestamps to seismic_error.log; the program must accept a command‑line option ‑a to specify the I2C address (defaulting to the documented value), ‑i to set the sampling interval in seconds (default 1 s), and ‑f to set the output filename (default seismic_data.csv), perform reads at the configured interval, check every I2C read/write return value, retry transient failures up to three times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the ambient light from a BH1750 light sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, converts the 16‑bit big‑endian raw value to a floating‑point lux value, and broadcasts that value as a floating‑point string via UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with a TTL of 1; the program must check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs it should print an error message and retry after one second, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the socket before exiting, using only the Linux I2C ioctl interface and standard POSIX sockets, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/ttyS0) at 921600 baud, reads the sensor’s data stream, synchronizes on the documented 8‑byte little‑endian magic word, validates each TLV payload, extracts the range (in meters) and velocity (in meters per second) for every detected object, and appends rows to a file named radar_data.csv with the columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps; the program must check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, log any errors to stderr without crashing, and on all exit paths including SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing the UART using the provided driver library, flushing and closing the CSV file, and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that periodically reads range‑detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0, GPIO14/GPIO15 BCM pins as TXD/RXD) at 115200 baud, 8N1, using a 0.5 second inter‑byte timeout and a select() call with a 2‑second timeout to detect sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions; the program must open and configure the UART in non‑canonical mode, accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parse only complete newline‑terminated ASCII lines of the form `<unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters>\n`, and for each valid detection log to stdout exactly as “Timestamp: YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters”, while checking the result of every system call (open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup) and printing errno‑based diagnostics on failure, and must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a graceful shutdown that closes the UART on all exit paths, using only standard POSIX C libraries such as stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the Keywish 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (KY‑033) connected on the GPIO bus, configuring the left sensor pin as GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), the middle sensor pin as GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) and the right sensor pin as GPIO27 (BCM, physical pin 13) as inputs with pull‑up resistors enabled, noting that each sensor output is digital LOW when an obstacle is present and HIGH when clear, and runs a main loop at 10 Hz (100 ms period) that logs the three sensor states to the console with a timestamp using 0 for obstacle detected and 1 for clear, and when all three sensors read 0 the program must send the string “EMERGENCY STOP!\n” over the library’s API call to the UART device /dev/ttyAMA0 configured at 115200 baud, 8N1 with no flow control; the program must check the driver library initialization and, on failure, print an error and exit with code 1, while any failure of the API call should be reported with an error message but the program must continue running, handling write errors gracefully by printing the error without exiting; signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must close the UART port, terminate the driver library and release all resources before exiting, and any error path must also clean up all allocated resources.
